flashcards.q: What are the three moving parts of the backtracking skeleton?
flashcards.a: Choose (mutate shared state), explore (recurse), unchoose (undo the mutation so sibling branches start clean).

flashcards.q: What is the single most common backtracking bug?
flashcards.a: Forgetting to unchoose (undo the mutation) after the recursive call returns, letting state leak across sibling branches.

flashcards.q: Why must you record path[:] (a copy) rather than the live path reference into the result list?
flashcards.a: The path is mutated in place throughout the search; appending the live reference means every recorded answer is the same object, silently corrupted by later mutations.

flashcards.q: What is the key efficiency difference between pruning before recursing versus validating a completed candidate?
flashcards.a: Pruning before recursing abandons an invalid partial solution immediately, skipping the entire invalid subtree beneath it; validating only at the end pays the full exponential cost before discovering most branches were invalid.

flashcards.q: N-Queens (LC 51): what three sets do you track to prune before placing a queen, and roughly how much does it help for 8-Queens?
flashcards.a: Occupied columns, and both diagonals (row-col and row+col, each constant along one diagonal). Cuts explored states from billions of raw placements to roughly 2,057.

flashcards.q: Combination Sum (LC 39) vs Combination Sum II (LC 40): what index do you recurse with, and why?
flashcards.a: LC39 (unlimited reuse): recurse with the SAME index i. LC40 (each used once, duplicates in input): recurse with i+1 and skip duplicate values at the same recursion depth to avoid duplicate output.

flashcards.q: Does pruning change backtracking's worst-case asymptotic complexity?
flashcards.a: No -- the problems remain fundamentally exponential; pruning reduces the practically explored fraction of the search space, not the theoretical worst-case bound.

flashcards.q: Would you hand-roll backtracking for a real production scheduling/constraint system?
flashcards.a: No -- use a dedicated CP/SAT solver (OR-Tools CP-SAT, Z3) which implements far more sophisticated pruning (constraint propagation, conflict-driven learning) than hand-rolled recursive search.
